questions.prompt: A test double that returns canned answers and records nothing is called what?
hints: It only supplies answers.
Think of a stand-in with one line to say.
questions.onCorrect: A stub is the simplest double, for the case where the code under test needs only an answer.

choices.label: A stub
A fake
A spy
A mock

misconceptions.feedback: A mock records the calls it gets so the test can check them.
A fake has a working simple implementation, such as an in-memory repository.
A spy records calls like a mock but is usually a real object wrapped to watch it.

questions.prompt: A rule allows a discount when `10 <= quantity <= 99`. How many boundary test cases does it need at its two ends together, taking the value just outside and the value inside at each end?
hints: The rule has two boundaries.
Each boundary needs a value on each side.
Two cases for each end.
questions.onCorrect: Each end of a range is a boundary of its own and needs its own pair of cases.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cases are 9 and 10 at the lower end and 99 and 100 at the upper end, so 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That covers one boundary. The rule has two.
Each boundary needs a pair of cases, so the count is even.

questions.prompt: A system has four layers: presentation, application, domain and data. In a strict design each layer may depend only on the layer directly below it. How many dependency arrows between layers are allowed?
hints: Each layer except the lowest has exactly one layer below it.
Count the layers that have a layer below.
Four layers, and the lowest has nothing below.
questions.onCorrect: Three arrows, and a relaxed design that lets any layer call any layer below it allows more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Presentation to application, application to domain and domain to data make 3.

misconceptions.feedback: The lowest layer has nothing below it, so it has no arrow.
That is the relaxed count, where a layer may also skip layers.

questions.prompt: A relaxed design has five layers, and each layer may depend on every layer below it. How many dependency arrows are allowed?
hints: Each pair of layers allows one arrow, from the upper to the lower one.
This is the same count as the links between modules.
questions.onCorrect: Ten arrows, so relaxing the rule multiplies the places where a change can spread.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each pair of layers allows one arrow, from the upper to the lower, so 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strict count. Here a layer may reach any layer below it.
That counts each pair twice. Only the upper layer depends on the lower one.

questions.prompt: The domain needs to send receipts, so it defines a ReceiptSender interface with one method, send, that says in its own words what it needs. In ports and adapters, what is ReceiptSender?
hints: The domain defines it and the outside world plugs into it.
A harbour has them too.
questions.onCorrect: The port belongs to the domain, so whatever actually sends the receipts depends on the domain and not the other way round.

misconceptions.feedback: An adapter is the piece that connects to the real system. The question asks about the interface the domain owns.
An interface is the right kind of thing, but this architecture style gives an interface that the domain owns a more specific name.

questions.prompt: The function `total_with_tax(price, rate_port)` returns `price + price * rate_port()`, where `rate_port` is a function that returns the tax rate. What does `print(total_with_tax(100, lambda: 0.2))` show?
hints: The port returns the tax rate.
Work out the tax on 100 at that rate.
Add the tax to the price.
questions.onCorrect: The function got its rate from outside, so a test can pass lambda: 0.0 and expect 100.0.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the tax alone. The function adds it to the price.
That would be the result with a rate of 0.

questions.prompt: A class SmtpReceiptSender implements the domain's ReceiptSender interface by talking to a real mail server. In ports and adapters, what is SmtpReceiptSender?
hints: It adapts the mail server to the port's shape.
One of the patterns from an earlier lesson has this name.
questions.onCorrect: The mail adapter imports the domain's port, so the dependency arrow points inward.

misconceptions.feedback: The port is the domain's interface. The piece that connects it to the database has another name.
It does implement the interface the domain owns, and this architecture style gives the piece that connects that interface to the outside system a more specific name.

questions.prompt: A project's imports are: web adapter imports domain; domain imports the web framework; database adapter imports the domain's port; domain imports the database library; a test imports domain. How many of these imports break the dependency rule?
hints: The rule is that dependencies point inward, toward the domain.
An import by the domain of something outside points outward.
Count the imports in which the domain is the importer of an outside library.
questions.onCorrect: Two imports point outward, and both can be removed by giving the domain a port instead.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The domain importing the web framework and the domain importing the database library point outward, so 2 break the rule.

misconceptions.feedback: A test importing the domain points inward, which the rule allows.
Both the web framework and the database library are outside the domain.

questions.prompt: A domain module begins with `import sqlalchemy`, a database library. Which rule does that line break?
hints: Source-code dependencies must point in a certain direction.
Ask whether the domain should need a database library in order to run.
questions.onCorrect: The domain now cannot be built or tested without that library, though it should know nothing of storage.

misconceptions.feedback: The rule of three says when to remove repeated code. Nothing is repeated here, and the fault is the direction of an import.
That principle concerns a subtype standing in for its base type. This line breaks a rule about which way imports point.
YAGNI warns against building for needs that do not exist yet. This import is a real dependency, and it points outward from the domain.

choices.label: The Liskov substitution principle
The rule of three
YAGNI
The dependency rule

questions.prompt: Using `total_with_tax` from the lesson, what does `print(total_with_tax(250, lambda: 0.1))` output?
hints: Work out the tax first.
The tax is the price times the rate.
Add it to the price.
questions.onCorrect: The rate arrived through the port, so a test can choose any rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the tax alone.
That adds 10 rather than 10% of the price.

questions.prompt: A relaxed design has six layers, and each may depend on every layer below it. How many dependency arrows are allowed?
hints: Each pair of layers allows one arrow.
Six layers.
questions.onCorrect: Fifteen arrows, against five in a strict design.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strict count.
That counts every pair twice.

questions.prompt: Which finding breaks the dependency rule?
hints: Ask which import points away from the domain.
The domain should know nothing of frameworks.
questions.onCorrect: A framework import in the domain ties the core to a detail that should be replaceable.

choices.label: The web adapter imports the domain
The domain module imports the web framework
A test imports the domain
The database adapter imports the domain port

acceptedIdeas: The domain module imports the web framework
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The domain module imports the web framework

misconceptions.feedback: An adapter pointing inward at the domain is what the rule asks for.
The adapter depends on the port that the domain owns, which is the correct direction.
A test is outside the domain, so importing it points inward.

questions.prompt: A request passes through five services in sequence. Each is 99.9% available, and they fail independently. Roughly how available is the whole chain?
hints: The request needs every one of the five to be up at the same moment.

choices.label: More, about 99.99%, since the services back each other up
A little less, about 99.5%
Much less, about 95%
The same as one service, 99.9%

questions.onCorrect: Each service adds a small chance of failure, and five of them multiply to about 0.995.

misconceptions.feedback: Each service can be down at a different moment, and the request fails whenever any one of them is, so the chain cannot match a single service.
The fall is real but small: each service is down only a thousandth of the time, so five of them lose about five thousandths together.
The services here are in sequence, not alternatives, so none of them can stand in for another when it is down.

questions.prompt: A request passes through ten services in sequence, each 99.9% available, and they fail independently. To one decimal place, what is the availability of the chain, in percent?
hints: The chain needs every service in it to be up.
Multiply the availability by itself, once for each service.
The result is a little under the figure for five services.
questions.onCorrect: Ten services give 99.0%, which is about seven hours of downtime in a month.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.999 to the power 10 is 0.990, or 99.0%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one service. Every further service in the chain lowers the figure.
That is the figure for five services, and this chain is longer.

questions.prompt: A company has three teams that rarely talk to one another, and the product they build ends up as three parts joined by thin interfaces exactly where the teams meet. The law that predicts this is named after whom?
hints: The paper was called How Do Committees Invent?
It appeared in Datamation in April 1968.
questions.onCorrect: Melvin Conway published the observation in 1968, and the name Conway's law was given to it later.

misconceptions.feedback: Parkinson's law is about work expanding to fill the time. This one is about structure mirroring communication.

questions.prompt: A team of five is starting a booking system for a client who has not yet settled which features it needs or how they divide. Which is the sensible starting point?
hints: The boundaries are not yet known.
Choose the shape that is cheapest to change.
questions.onCorrect: A modular monolith keeps boundaries enforced but cheap to move, and a module can be split into a service when a measured reason appears.

choices.label: A separate service per developer
A modular monolith
One shared database for every product
Twenty microservices

misconceptions.feedback: Twenty services for five people multiply operations and network failures before the boundaries are known.
A shared database couples every product to the same tables.
A service per developer fixes boundaries by headcount, which has nothing to do with the domain.

questions.prompt: A chain is 99.5% available. In a 30-day month of 720 hours, for how many hours is it unavailable?
hints: Unavailability is what remains after availability.
That is 0.5%.
Take 0.5% of 720 hours.
questions.onCorrect: About three and a half hours a month, from five services that each looked reliable on its own.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.5% of 720 hours is 0.005 × 720 = 3.6 hours.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time the chain is available. The question asks for the time it is not.
0.5 is the percentage that is unavailable. Apply it to the 720 hours.

questions.prompt: A chain has four services, each 99.5% available and independent. To one decimal place, what is the availability of the chain in percent?
hints: Multiply the availabilities of all four.
Raise the availability to the power of the number of services.
The result is lower than the availability of any single service.
questions.onCorrect: Four weaker services give 98.0%, which is lower than ten services of 99.9% gave.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.995 to the power 4 is 0.980, or 98.0%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the availability of one service. All four are needed.
That is above the true value. Each service loses a share of what the previous one left.

questions.prompt: Four services in sequence are each 99.9% available. To one decimal place, what is the chain's availability, in percent?
hints: Multiply 0.999 by itself.
Do it four times.
The result is a little under 99.7.
questions.onCorrect: Each added service lowers the chain by a little under its own failure rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.999 to the power 4 is 0.996, or 99.6%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one service. All four must work.
That is the figure for three services.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses Conway's law?
hints: It concerns the shape of the system and the shape of the organisation.
It dates from 1968.
questions.onCorrect: Conway's observation is why teams and services tend to line up, and why teams can be shaped to the architecture wanted.

choices.label: Systems copy the structure of the database that stores their data
Systems copy the communication structure of the organisation that builds them
Systems copy the structure of the problem they were built to solve
Systems grow until they match the size of the largest team that works on them

acceptedIdeas: Systems copy the communication structure of the organisation that builds them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Systems copy the communication structure of the organisation that builds them

misconceptions.feedback: A database may constrain a design, but Conway's observation is about the organisation that builds the system.
A design that follows the problem is what domain modelling aims at. Conway observed that designs follow the communication lines of the people who build them.
Team size is not the pattern Conway noticed. His observation concerns who talks to whom.

questions.prompt: What is a single deployable unit whose code is divided into modules with enforced boundaries called?
hints: It is one unit with internal structure.
Two words: the first says how it is divided.
questions.onCorrect: Its boundaries are enforced inside one process, so a module can later become a service.

misconceptions.feedback: Microservices are separately deployed. This is one unit.

questions.prompt: An account's events are deposit 50, withdraw 20 and deposit 5, in that order, starting from 0. What is the balance after the events are replayed?
hints: Start from 0 and apply the events in order.
A deposit adds and a withdrawal subtracts.
Keep a running balance after each event.
questions.onCorrect: The balance is not stored anywhere. It is whatever the events add up to.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every amount, including the withdrawal.
That stops before the last deposit.

questions.prompt: ReleaseStock is a message sent to the stock service, asking it to free goods it set aside earlier, and the stock service may refuse. Is it a command or an event?
hints: Can the receiver refuse it?
Names in the imperative, such as PlaceOrder, ask for something.
questions.onCorrect: A command is named in the imperative because it asks, while an event such as StockReleased is named in the past tense.

acceptedIdeas: A command, because it asks for something and may be refused
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A command, because it asks for something and may be refused

misconceptions.feedback: An event is announced to whoever is listening and cannot be refused. A message addressed to one receiver that may refuse it is a command.
What a message is about does not decide its kind. What decides it is whether the message asks for something or records that something has happened.

choices.label: An event, because it is sent to the stock service
A command, because it asks for something and may be refused
An event, because it concerns the state of the stock

questions.prompt: An order flow has a few steps that are unlikely to change, and the team wants to read and debug the whole flow in one place. Which style suits it, and what does that style cost?
hints: Ask which style keeps the steps in one place.
A single place that knows what happens next is also a single place that every flow needs.
questions.onCorrect: An orchestrator holds the steps in one place, so the flow is easy to follow and a failure can be handled there, but every flow depends on that central service.

acceptedIdeas: Orchestration, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orchestration, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on

misconceptions.feedback: A central service that every flow depends on is the price of orchestration. In choreography there is none, but nobody holds the whole flow.
Choreography couples services loosely, but the flow is visible only in the events as they pass, which makes it harder to follow and to debug.
The coordinator is a service that every flow depends on, and that dependence is a cost.

choices.label: Orchestration, at no price, since the steps are written in one place
Orchestration, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on
Choreography, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on
Choreography, at no price, since each service only reacts to events

questions.prompt: An account's events are deposit 100, withdraw 30 and withdraw 45, in that order, from 0. What is the balance after replay?
hints: Replay the events in order from 0.
Deposits add and withdrawals subtract.
Subtract both withdrawals from the deposit.
questions.onCorrect: Replay gives 25, and replaying only the first two events would have given 70, which is the balance at that earlier time.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the withdrawals instead of subtracting them.
That stops after the first withdrawal. There is another event.

questions.prompt: The events are deposit 200, withdraw 75, deposit 25 and withdraw 60. What is the balance after replay?
hints: Keep a running balance.
After the first two events it is 125.
Apply the last two events to the running balance.
questions.onCorrect: The running balance at each step is also available, which is how a past state can be read.

misconceptions.feedback: That stops before the final withdrawal.
That adds every amount. Withdrawals subtract.

questions.prompt: A shop serves its product pages from a table shaped for display, and that table is updated from events published by the code that checks and saves changes to products. What four-letter name is given to this split?
hints: It names commands and queries.
It stands for command query responsibility segregation.
questions.onCorrect: CQRS lets the read side be shaped for screens while the write side guards the rules.

misconceptions.feedback: Event sourcing stores state as events. This is about splitting the models for writing and reading.

questions.prompt: The events are deposit 50, withdraw 20 and deposit 5, but a retry stored the last deposit twice, so the log holds four events. What does a replay give?
hints: The log now holds four events.
The duplicate deposit is applied as well.
Add the second deposit to the usual result.
questions.onCorrect: A duplicated event is applied twice unless each event has an id that the consumer checks.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the duplicate. A replay applies every event it finds.
That counts the duplicate as 10. Each copy of the deposit is 5.

questions.prompt: An account's events are deposit 100, withdraw 30 and deposit 15. What is the balance after replay?
hints: Replay from 0.
Subtract the withdrawal.
Add the last deposit.
questions.onCorrect: The same log always gives the same balance.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the withdrawal. It subtracts.
That stops before the last deposit.

questions.prompt: In which style does a central coordinator tell each service what to do?
hints: One service knows all the steps.
It conducts, like an orchestra.
questions.onCorrect: The coordinator knows the order of the steps, so a failed step can be handled in one place.

choices.label: Orchestration
Choreography
Event sourcing
CQRS

misconceptions.feedback: In choreography nobody coordinates, and services react to events.
Event sourcing concerns how state is stored, not who coordinates.
CQRS concerns separate models for reading and writing.

questions.prompt: In which tense is the name of an event, such as OrderPlaced, written?
hints: An event records something that has happened.
Think of OrderPlaced.
questions.onCorrect: The past tense signals that the event is a fact, and a fact cannot be refused.

misconceptions.feedback: Present-tense and imperative names suggest a request. An event is a record of something finished.

questions.prompt: The function `read(msg)` parses a JSON message into `d` and returns `d.get('qty', 1) * d['price']`. What does `print(read('{"price": 4, "extra": true}'))` show?
hints: get returns the default when the key is missing.
The default quantity is 1.
Multiply the quantity by the price.
questions.onCorrect: The reader copes with a missing field and an unknown one, so the message still works.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The message has no `qty`, so `get` returns the default 1, and 1 × 4 = 4. The `extra` field is ignored.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the default quantity. The function multiplies it by the price.
The price is present, so the result is not zero.

questions.prompt: A provider renames the field price to cost and stops sending price. Three existing clients each read price. What happens to them?
hints: Ask which clients read the field being renamed.
A client keeps working only while the name it looks up still exists.
questions.onCorrect: Every client breaks, because price is the one field they all read.

acceptedIdeas: All three break, because each looks the field up by its old name
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All three break, because each looks the field up by its old name

misconceptions.feedback: A tolerant reader ignores extra fields and defaults missing ones, but price is a field these clients read, so without it they have nothing to work with.
A client that supplies a default does not stop, but it now computes with the wrong value. Either way it has lost the field it reads.
An announcement does not change the clients' code, which still asks for price. They fail on the day the name goes unless they are edited first.

choices.label: None of them break, because tolerant readers ignore fields they do not know
All three break, because each looks the field up by its old name
None of them break, as long as the provider announces the change first
Only the clients that treat a missing field as an error

questions.prompt: A mobile app takes the name and price from each product message, ignores every other field, and shows a stock picture when the image field is missing. Which kind of reader is it?
hints: It tolerates change in the message.
Its name describes how it reads.
questions.onCorrect: A tolerant reader survives the additions that would otherwise break strict clients.

misconceptions.feedback: A strict reader rejects unknown fields. This one accepts them.

questions.prompt: Which change is backwards compatible for existing clients?
hints: Which change leaves everything the clients already use in place?
The new field must not be required.
questions.onCorrect: An added optional field leaves every existing field alone, unless a client rejects unknown fields.

choices.label: Removing a field
Requiring a new field in requests
Renaming a field
Adding an optional field to a response

acceptedIdeas: Adding an optional field to a response
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adding an optional field to a response

misconceptions.feedback: A client that asks for the old name no longer finds it.
A client that reads the field fails when it is gone.
Clients that omit the new field are now rejected.

questions.prompt: A provider is renaming qty to quantity with expand and contract. There are 5 clients, and 2 have moved to quantity. How many must still move before qty can be removed?
hints: The old name can go only when no client reads it.
Count the clients that have not yet moved.
Subtract the clients that moved from the total.
questions.onCorrect: Three clients, and until they move the old name has to stay.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 − 2 = 3 clients still read `qty`.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number that have moved. The question asks how many have not.
That is the total. Two have moved already.

questions.prompt: A provider makes currency a required field in requests, and clients that never sent it are now rejected. What kind of change is this?
hints: Ask whether a correct existing client still works after the change.
A new requirement can break a client even when no field is removed.
questions.onCorrect: A new required field makes every client that omits it fail, so it breaks them even though no field was removed.

acceptedIdeas: Breaking, because correct existing clients now fail
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breaking, because correct existing clients now fail

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing was renamed or removed, but a requirement was added. Clients that never sent currency are rejected, so correct existing clients fail.
Clients would have to add it before the change, not after it. From the day it is required, every client that omits it is rejected.

choices.label: Breaking, because correct existing clients now fail
Compatible, because clients can add the field whenever they like
Compatible, because no field was renamed or removed

questions.prompt: With `read` as in the lesson, what does `print(read('{"price": 5, "qty": 3, "extra": 1}'))` output?
hints: The message carries a qty this time.
Multiply the quantity by the price.
Ignore the extra field.
questions.onCorrect: A tolerant reader uses what it knows and ignores the rest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `qty` is 3 and `price` is 5, so the result is 3 × 5 = 15. The `extra` field is ignored.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the default quantity. The message contains qty.
That adds the two. The function multiplies them.

questions.prompt: What is the safe order for renaming a field with expand and contract?
hints: The old name must stay until nobody reads it.
Three steps.
questions.onCorrect: At every step each client has a name it can read, which is why nothing breaks.

choices.label: Remove the old name, add the new name, then migrate clients
Migrate clients, add the new name, then remove the old name
Add the new name, remove the old name, then migrate clients
Add the new name, migrate clients, then remove the old name

acceptedIdeas: Add the new name, migrate clients, then remove the old name
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add the new name, migrate clients, then remove the old name

misconceptions.feedback: Removing first breaks every client that reads the old name.
Clients cannot migrate to a name that does not exist yet.
Removing the old name before the clients have moved breaks every client that still reads it.

questions.prompt: Five changes are proposed: rename a field, remove a field, add an optional response field, change a field's type, and add an endpoint. How many of them are breaking?
hints: Which of the five make a correct existing client fail?
Additions leave existing fields alone.
Rename, remove and change a type are the ones that touch a field.
questions.onCorrect: Additions are usually safe and alterations are not, with the exception of strict clients.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Renaming, removing and changing a type are breaking, which makes 3. Adding an optional field and adding an endpoint are not.

misconceptions.feedback: Two of the five are additions. The other three alter or remove something.
Adding an optional field and adding an endpoint leave existing clients working.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows the shop as a single box. Around it are the customers who use it and the payment provider it calls. Which C4 level is it?
hints: The system is not opened up.
The picture is about what lies around it.
questions.onCorrect: The context level treats the system as one box, so it can be shown to anyone, including people who will never read code.

choices.label: Containers
Code
Components
System context

misconceptions.feedback: A container diagram opens the system into its separately runnable parts. Here the system stays one box.
Components are the parts inside one container. Nothing here is inside the system.
Code is the lowest level, with classes and functions.

questions.prompt: A diagram of a ticket system shows its mobile app, its booking API and its database as separate boxes joined by labelled arrows. Which C4 level is it?
hints: The parts are the separately runnable units.
The second level.
questions.onCorrect: Level 2 answers what the main building blocks are and how they talk, which suits developers and operations.

misconceptions.feedback: Components are the parts inside one container, which is the next level down.

questions.prompt: A level 2 diagram is drawn for a system made of a web app, a mobile app, an API, a database and a message broker. Which of these does it show as containers?
hints: A C4 container is not a Docker container.
Each part that is runnable or holds data counts, including a database.
questions.onCorrect: A database is a container in C4, because it is something that has to be running for the system to work.

acceptedIdeas: All five, because each is a separately runnable unit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All five, because each is a separately runnable unit

misconceptions.feedback: A C4 container is any separately runnable unit, and a database has to be running for the system to work, so it is a container too.
A container here is not a Docker container. The same unit may or may not be run in one, and either way it is shown.
The web app, the mobile app, the database and the broker are all parts of the system, and each is separately runnable, so each is a container.

choices.label: Only the web app, the mobile app and the API, because a database is not a program
Only the parts that are run in Docker
All five, because each is a separately runnable unit
Only the API, since the others are outside the system

questions.prompt: A diagram has 7 arrows, and 3 of them carry a label. How many arrows still need one?
hints: Every arrow should say what it carries.
Count the arrows that have no label.
Subtract the labelled arrows from all of them.
questions.onCorrect: Four arrows still leave the reader to guess whether they are requests, events or copies.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 7 − 3 = 4 arrows have no label.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number already labelled. The question asks how many still need one.
That is the total number of arrows.

questions.prompt: A new developer needs to see which services make up the system and how they communicate. Which C4 level fits best?
hints: The services are the separately runnable parts.
Pick the level that opens the system once.
questions.onCorrect: Containers is the usual starting point for developers joining a team, and components can be added for the one they will work in.

choices.label: Containers
System context
Code
Components

misconceptions.feedback: Context treats the system as one box, so the services do not appear.
Components are the parts inside a single container, and she first needs the whole picture of the system.
Code is too detailed for a first view of the system.

questions.prompt: How many levels does the C4 model define?
hints: List them from the widest view to the narrowest.
Context is the first.
Code is the last.
questions.onCorrect: The fourth level, code, is rarely drawn by hand because it can be generated from the source.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The levels are context, containers, components and code: 4.

misconceptions.feedback: There is a fourth level, code, below components.
There are four, not five.

questions.prompt: In C4, what is a container?
hints: It is a unit that must be running or present for the system to work.
The word is not about Docker.
questions.onCorrect: The C4 container is a deployment-neutral idea of a runnable or data-holding unit.

choices.label: A Docker image that holds the system's code
A class or module inside one component
A separately runnable unit, such as a database
A physical server rack in a data centre

acceptedIdeas: A separately runnable unit, such as a database
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A separately runnable unit, such as a database

misconceptions.feedback: A container may be run as a Docker container, but the C4 word covers anything separately runnable, such as a mobile app.
Classes are code-level elements, far smaller than containers.
A rack is hardware, which belongs to a deployment view.

questions.prompt: Which C4 level shows the parts inside one container, such as a controller and a repository?
hints: It is the level between containers and code.
The third level.
questions.onCorrect: Components are drawn only for a container whose inner structure someone needs to understand.

misconceptions.feedback: Containers are the units of the whole system, one level above.

questions.prompt: A container diagram has a box for the part of the system that takes orders. Which label for the box follows the diagram hygiene rules?
hints: Each element needs three things.
Check each label for a name, a type and a short description.
questions.onCorrect: Only the first label has all three, and a few words of text spare the reader a good deal of guessing.

acceptedIdeas: Orders API, container: web API, takes orders and checks stock
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Orders API, container: web API, takes orders and checks stock

misconceptions.feedback: A bare name does not say what kind of element the box is or what it does, so the reader has to guess.
It has a name and a type but no short description, so the reader cannot tell what the box does.
It has a name and a description but no type, so the reader cannot tell whether it is a program, a table or a team.

choices.label: Orders API, container: web API, takes orders and checks stock
Orders API, container: web API
Service
Orders API, takes orders and checks stock

questions.prompt: Weights are performance 0.5, cost 0.3 and simplicity 0.2. Option A scores 8, 5 and 6 on those three criteria. What is A's weighted total?
hints: Multiply each score by its weight.
The three products are 4, 1.5 and 1.2.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: A scores 6.7 out of 10, and the weights decide how much each criterion counts toward it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scores without the weights.
That uses the wrong weight on one of the scores. Match each score to its own criterion.

questions.prompt: Weights are performance 0.5, cost 0.3 and simplicity 0.2. Option B scores 6, 9 and 9 on those three criteria. What is B's weighted total?
hints: Use the same weights as for A.
The three products are 3, 2.7 and 1.8.
Add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: B scores 7.5 against A's 6.7, so under these weights B ranks first.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scores without the weights.
That gives the wrong weight to one score. Match each score to its own criterion.

questions.prompt: Weights are now performance 0.6, cost 0.2 and simplicity 0.2. What is A's weighted total, if its scores are 8, 5 and 6?
hints: Multiply each score by its new weight.
The products are 4.8, 1 and 1.2.
Add the three.
questions.onCorrect: A rises to 7.0 as performance counts for more, and B rises only to 7.2.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A's total under the earlier weights.
That is B's total under these weights.

questions.prompt: In March a team records that orders are stored in PostgreSQL. In June a new record moves orders to a document store and names the March record as the one it replaces. Which status does the March record now take?
hints: The statuses are proposed, accepted, deprecated and one more.
The new record takes the place of the old.
questions.onCorrect: The old record is kept, with the status superseded and a link to the new one, so the history stays readable.

misconceptions.feedback: Deprecated means still in force but discouraged. A replaced decision has another status.

questions.prompt: A fitness function scans 40 domain modules and fails the build for each one that imports the web framework. It finds 3. What happens to the build?
hints: A fitness function turns a decision into a test.
Ask what a test does when even one case breaks the rule.
questions.onCorrect: The decision is enforced by the build itself, so the breach is found when it is made and not a year later.

acceptedIdeas: It fails, because even one breach is enough to stop the build
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fails, because even one breach is enough to stop the build

misconceptions.feedback: The check fails the build for each module that imports the framework, so a single breach is enough to stop it. The decision is enforced and not averaged.
A warning nobody has to act on is the situation the fitness function exists to avoid. It fails the build so that a breach is found when it is made.
The check has no majority threshold. It fails the build for each module that breaks the decision.

choices.label: It passes with a warning that someone may read later
It fails, because even one breach is enough to stop the build
It passes, because 37 of the 40 modules follow the decision
It fails only if more than half of the modules break the rule

questions.prompt: Cost and simplicity now matter most, with weights performance 0.2, cost 0.3 and simplicity 0.5. What is A's total, scoring 8, 5 and 6?
hints: Multiply each score by its weight.
The products are 1.6, 1.5 and 3.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: A scores 6.1 under these weights, and B would score 8.4, so the weights have changed the ranking by more than the scores could.

misconceptions.feedback: That is A's total under the first weights.
That adds the scores without the weights.

questions.prompt: Option C scores 4, 10 and 8, with weights performance 0.5, cost 0.3 and simplicity 0.2. What is C's weighted total?
hints: Multiply each score by its weight.
The products are 2, 3 and 1.6.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: C scores 6.6, below both A and B under these weights.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scores without the weights.
That averages the scores. Each must be multiplied by its own weight.

questions.prompt: An ADR is replaced by a later one. Which status does the old record take?
hints: The later record takes its place.
The statuses end with deprecated and one more.
questions.onCorrect: A superseded record stays in the repository so that the reasons for the change can be read.

choices.label: Accepted
Draft
Superseded
Proposed

misconceptions.feedback: Proposed is for a decision not yet taken.
The old record is no longer the accepted decision.
Draft is not one of the usual statuses, and the old record was a finished decision.

questions.prompt: What is an automated check that a chosen property still holds, such as that no domain module imports the web framework, called?
hints: It tests the architecture, not a feature.
Its name suggests it checks that the design is still fit.
questions.onCorrect: A fitness function turns a decision into a test, so a breach is found when it is made.

misconceptions.feedback: A unit test checks behaviour of code. This checks a property of the architecture.

questions.prompt: A module is used by 3 other modules and itself uses 1 other module. What fraction of all its dependency links point out from it, rather than in?
hints: Count all the links the module takes part in, in either direction.
That is 3 incoming and 1 outgoing.
Divide the outgoing links by all of them.
questions.onCorrect: A quarter of its links point out, which makes it hard to change because three modules rely on it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: It has 3 + 1 = 4 links in all, and 1 of them is outgoing, so the fraction is 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction of links that point in. The question asks about those pointing out.
That is the number of outgoing links, not the fraction of all links.

questions.prompt: A module has 1 incoming dependency (Ca) and 4 outgoing (Ce). What is its instability, Ce ÷ (Ca + Ce)?
hints: Ce is the outgoing count and Ca the incoming count.
Add them to get all the links.
Divide Ce by that total.
questions.onCorrect: At 0.8 it is unstable, which is acceptable for a module that few others rely on.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction incoming. Instability counts the outgoing share.
That is Ce alone. Divide it by the total of Ca and Ce.

questions.prompt: A shortcut saves 6 hours now but adds 1 hour to every later change. After how many later changes has the shortcut cost as much extra time as it saved?
hints: Each later change adds an hour.
The interest has to reach the amount saved.
Divide the hours saved by the hours added per change.
questions.onCorrect: After six changes the shortcut has cost all that it saved, and every change after that is pure interest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each later change costs 1 hour, so 6 changes cost 6 hours, which equals the 6 hours saved.

misconceptions.feedback: One change costs only 1 hour, which is far short of what the shortcut saved.
At 7 changes the shortcut is already behind. It breaks even at the sixth.

questions.prompt: A repair would cost 10 hours once. The shortcut it would remove adds 1 hour to each change, and the team makes 4 changes a month. After how many months has the repair paid for itself?
hints: Work out the hours the shortcut costs each month.
That is 4 changes at 1 hour each.
Divide the repair's cost by the monthly cost.
questions.onCorrect: After two and a half months the repair is cheaper than living with the shortcut, which is a measurable reason to do it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shortcut costs 1 × 4 = 4 hours a month, so the 10-hour repair pays for itself after 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5 months.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the repair cost in hours. Divide by the monthly cost of the shortcut.
That is the hours lost each month. Divide the repair cost by it.

questions.prompt: A system has 8 slices of functionality, and 3 of them have been routed to the new system by the strangler approach. What is true of the system at this point?
hints: The router sends each slice to the system where it now lives.
The pattern's strength is that the system works at every stage.
questions.onCorrect: Each slice lives in exactly one system, so 5 are still in the old one and the whole keeps working while the rest move.

acceptedIdeas: It works, with 3 slices in the new system and 5 in the old one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It works, with 3 slices in the new system and 5 in the old one

misconceptions.feedback: The router sends each slice to wherever it now lives, so the 5 unmoved slices are still served by the old system and the whole keeps working.
The old system is retired only when it has no work left, and 5 slices still depend on it.
The router sends a request for a slice to one system, the one where that slice now lives.

choices.label: Both systems answer every request, and the faster reply is used
It is broken until the remaining 5 slices have moved
It works, with 3 slices in the new system and 5 in the old one
The old system can be retired, because the new one is running

questions.prompt: Before refactoring an untested pricing function, you run it on 50 sample orders and write tests that assert whatever it returns today, including one result that looks wrong. What are these tests called?
hints: It captures the current behaviour, right or wrong.
The name is about describing what the code is like.
questions.onCorrect: A characterisation test lets unintended changes be detected when code has no tests of its own.

misconceptions.feedback: A unit test checks intended behaviour. This kind records what happens now, whatever it is.

questions.prompt: Checkout and orders have both been moved to the new system, and reports are still in the old one. A request for orders arrives at the router. Where does the router send it?
hints: The router sends each slice to the system where that slice now lives.
Ask where orders lives now.
questions.onCorrect: Orders now lives in the new system, so the router sends its requests there while reports still goes to the old one.

acceptedIdeas: To the new system, because orders has been moved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: To the new system, because orders has been moved

misconceptions.feedback: The router decides by slice and not by order of arrival. Orders has moved, so the request goes to the new system.
Reports has no bearing on a request for orders. The router decides by the slice that is requested.
A request goes to one system, the one where its slice now lives.

choices.label: To the new system, because orders has been moved
To both systems, and it uses the faster reply
To the old system, because the router always tries the old system first
To the old system, because reports is still there

questions.prompt: A module has 2 incoming and 2 outgoing dependencies. What is its instability, Ce ÷ (Ca + Ce)?
hints: Add the two counts.
Divide the outgoing count by the total.
Half of the links point out.
questions.onCorrect: A value in the middle shows a module that is neither a stable base nor a free-standing leaf.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the instability of a module with no incoming links.
That is the outgoing count. Divide it by the total.

questions.prompt: In the strangler pattern, how is the old system replaced?
hints: A router sends each slice somewhere.
Think of a vine growing over a tree.
questions.onCorrect: The old system keeps working throughout, and each slice moves when it is ready.

choices.label: By moving one slice at a time to the new system through a router
By building the new system alongside it and switching everything on a launch day
By running both systems side by side for ever and never retiring the old one
By deleting the old system's code one module at a time before the new code exists

acceptedIdeas: By moving one slice at a time to the new system through a router
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: By moving one slice at a time to the new system through a router

misconceptions.feedback: A single launch day is the big-bang rewrite that the strangler pattern is designed to avoid.
The aim is to retire the old system once it has no work left.
Deleting first would leave parts of the system with nothing running them while the new system is built.

questions.prompt: What is changing the structure of code without changing its behaviour, protected by tests, called?
hints: The behaviour stays the same.
It is the word for restructuring code.
questions.onCorrect: Refactoring in small steps, with the tests passing after each, makes it a part of ordinary feature work.

misconceptions.feedback: A rewrite replaces the code and may change the behaviour. This keeps the behaviour and changes the structure.

questions.prompt: A service keeps its customers in a table with a column called `cust`, and only that service reads the table. The column is renamed `customer_id`, and the service's responses to its callers stay exactly the same. What has to change?
hints: Ask which code has the column name written into it.
questions.onCorrect: Only the service has the column name written into its code, so the rename is one edit in one place.

choices.label: The service and every program that calls it
Only the service's own code
Nothing, since a column name is only a label

misconceptions.feedback: The callers see only the service's responses, and those have not changed, so they cannot tell that the column was renamed.
The service's queries name the column, so they fail until they are edited.

questions.prompt: Four changes are proposed to a system that other teams build on. Once those teams depend on it, which is the hardest to reverse?
hints: Ask how many other programs have to change when each decision is undone.
Programs outside your code cannot be edited in the same commit.

acceptedIdeas: Changing the file format that nine programs read and write
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Changing the file format that nine programs read and write

questions.onCorrect: Nine programs have copied the file format into their own code, so undoing it means asking each of them to change.

choices.label: Renaming a column in a table that only one service reads
Replacing the sorting routine inside one module
Changing the file format that nine programs read and write
Renaming a helper function that two files call

misconceptions.feedback: Only the service that reads the table has the name in its code, so the change stays inside one program.
A routine inside one module is called from that module only, so no other program notices the change.
Two files in one project can be edited together in one commit, so the change reaches nobody outside.

questions.prompt: The measure says 99.9% of requests must succeed. Why does the example take 99.9% away from 100% before it finds the allowance?
hints: What does the test count?

acceptedIdeas: The test counts failures, so it needs the share the measure leaves for them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The test counts failures, so it needs the share the measure leaves for them

questions.onCorrect: The measure states what must go right, and a test can only count what goes wrong, so the allowance is the share that is left over.

choices.label: The test counts failures, so it needs the share the measure leaves for them
A percentage has to be taken away from 100% before it is used on a count
The measure is written the wrong way round, so it has to be turned over
One of the two servers is down, so 0.1% of the requests are lost

misconceptions.feedback: A percentage of a count can be taken directly. The subtraction is here because the test needs the share that may fail.
The measure is written correctly: it states the share that must succeed. The example turns it into the share that may fail because that is what a test counts.
The environment says what the system is doing when the requests arrive. It does not remove any requests from the measure.

questions.prompt: A team has three open decisions: the colour scheme of an internal admin screen, the format of the events that six other services will read, and the name of a variable inside one function. They have time to settle only one before coding starts. Which should it be?
hints: Ask which decision other services would start to depend on.
Pick the one that is costly to undo.

acceptedIdeas: The format of the events six other services will read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The format of the events six other services will read

questions.onCorrect: Six services will copy the event format into their own code, which makes it costly to undo.

choices.label: The format of the events six other services will read
The colour scheme of the internal admin screen
The name of the variable inside one function
Whichever the team finds easiest to agree on

misconceptions.feedback: A colour scheme in one screen can be changed in an afternoon without asking anyone, so it can wait.
A local name is visible to one function, so renaming it later costs very little.
Ease of agreement says nothing about the cost of undoing a decision. Care should follow the cost of reversal.

questions.prompt: The author of a `Queue` changes it so that items come out newest first instead of oldest first. Every method name stays the same, yet callers that process jobs in the order they arrived break. Which part of the interface has changed?
hints: Think about which item a caller gets when it takes one out.
An interface covers names, ordering, errors and speed.

acceptedIdeas: The order in which items come out
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The order in which items come out

questions.onCorrect: A caller that expects oldest first breaks when the order flips, although no method name has changed.

choices.label: How fast each operation runs
The order in which items come out
The errors it reports
The names of the operations

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing about speed has changed. What changed is which item comes out first.
No error behaviour has changed. The items are the same, but they come out in a different order.
The names are unchanged, which is why this change catches callers by surprise.

questions.prompt: `Checkout` holds a `Notifier` and calls `notifier.send(message)` when an order is placed. A test has to run `Checkout` without sending any real message. What does the test have to do?
hints: `Checkout` calls `send` on whatever `Notifier` it holds.
Which object can the test supply without editing any existing class?

acceptedIdeas: Hand `Checkout` a small object with a `send` method that records messages
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hand `Checkout` a small object with a `send` method that records messages

questions.onCorrect: `Checkout` depends only on the `Notifier` interface, so the test supplies its own object with a `send` method and no existing class is edited.

choices.label: Edit `Checkout` so that it skips the call to `send` while the test runs
Edit `EmailNotifier` so that it does nothing while the test runs
Replace `Checkout` with a copy that never calls `send`
Hand `Checkout` a small object with a `send` method that records messages

misconceptions.feedback: That changes the code under test, so the test no longer shows how `Checkout` behaves. `Checkout` calls `send` on whatever it holds, and that is the place to substitute.
That changes a real class for the sake of one test. `Checkout` accepts any object with a `send` method, so a test can hand it a different one.
That tests a different class. The test should run the real `Checkout`.

questions.prompt: Three places in the code build a shipping label from the same four fields in the same way, and all three have to change whenever the label format changes. What does the rule of three say to do?
hints: The rule waits for a number of occurrences, and the number is in its name.
Ask whether the three copies change for the same reason.

acceptedIdeas: Write one shared function now, since the third copy has appeared
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Write one shared function now, since the third copy has appeared

questions.onCorrect: By the third copy the shared part is plain to see, so one function can hold it and a format change is made once.

choices.label: Write one shared function now, since the third copy has appeared
Wait for a fourth copy before writing anything shared
Leave all three alone, since repetition is harmless
Leave the copies and add a comment saying they must be kept in step

misconceptions.feedback: The rule names three, not four. The third appearance is the point at which the abstraction is written.
Repetition is tolerated at the second copy and not for ever, because every copy of the same knowledge needs its own edit when it changes.
A comment cannot keep three copies in step. By the third copy the common part is visible, and one function can hold it.

questions.prompt: A base class `Account` has `withdraw(amount)`. A subclass `FixedDeposit` overrides `withdraw` to raise an error, because money cannot be taken out before the term ends. A function that withdraws from every `Account` now crashes on a `FixedDeposit`. Which principle does `FixedDeposit` break?
hints: The subclass cannot be used wherever its base type is.
The principle concerns what a subtype must keep of its base type's promises.
questions.onCorrect: A `FixedDeposit` cannot stand in for an `Account`, so code written for `Account`s fails, and it is the hierarchy that has to change.

choices.label: Open-closed
Single responsibility
Liskov substitution
Dependency inversion

misconceptions.feedback: Open-closed is about adding behaviour without editing working code. The crash comes from a subtype that does not keep the promise of its base type.
That principle is about a class having several reasons to change. The fault lies in a subclass that refuses what its base class promised.
That principle is about which side owns an abstraction. The function already depends on `Account`, and the trouble is that one subtype does not behave as an `Account` does.

questions.prompt: A sender uses inheritance, with one subclass for each pair of transport and format, and it has 4 transports and 3 formats. A fourth format, YAML, is added. How many new subclasses does it need?
hints: The new format must work with every transport.
One subclass for each pairing of the new format with a transport.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new format has to work with each of the 4 transports, so it needs one subclass for each pairing: 4 new subclasses.

questions.onCorrect: Four new subclasses with inheritance, against one new class with composition, which is the gap that widens as the lists grow.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of subclasses that exist already. The question asks how many the new format adds.
That is the total once YAML is added. The question asks only for the new subclasses.
That is what composition needs, one class for the new format. With inheritance the format needs a subclass for each transport.

questions.prompt: A temperature sensor has to tell a display, a logger and an alarm whenever its reading changes, and the sensor should not know which of them exist. Which pattern fits?
hints: The sensor should announce, and others listen.
Which pattern keeps a list of listeners?
questions.onCorrect: Observer lets new listeners be added without editing the sensor, which stays unaware of what they do.

choices.label: Strategy
Observer
Adapter
Factory

misconceptions.feedback: A strategy swaps one algorithm behind a call. Here several parts need to react to the same change.
An adapter converts one interface into another, and nothing here needs converting.
A factory decides which class to create, which is not the problem.

questions.prompt: A team builds a plug-in system for report formats, with a registry, a loader and a configuration file. The product has one report format and nobody has asked for another. Which principle from the principles lesson names the mistake?
hints: Nothing varies yet, and nobody has asked for a second format.
One principle says not to build for a need you do not have yet.
questions.onCorrect: A plug-in system with one plug-in adds machinery that nothing uses.

choices.label: DRY
Liskov substitution
Single responsibility
YAGNI

misconceptions.feedback: DRY is about the same knowledge being written in more than one place. Here nothing is repeated.
Liskov concerns a subtype that cannot stand in for its base type. There is no subtype here.
Single responsibility is about a class with several reasons to change. The plug-in system is structure built for a need nobody has.

questions.prompt: Your code calls `logger.write(text)`, but the monitoring service your team adopts offers only `send_event(name, payload)`. Which pattern fits?
hints: Your code and the service disagree about an interface.
The pattern is named for fitting one thing to another.
questions.onCorrect: An adapter lets the monitoring service change without the rest of the program being edited.

choices.label: Singleton
Observer
Adapter
Factory

misconceptions.feedback: A singleton limits a class to one instance, which is a different problem.
Observer notifies many listeners. Here one call needs converting.
A factory chooses which class to create. Here the classes exist.

questions.prompt: A function `is_open()` returns `True` when the time is between 09:00 and 17:00. It reads the clock inside, so a test can see `True` only during opening hours. It is rewritten as `is_open(now)`, with the time passed in as an argument. What does the change give a test?
hints: The clock is a dependency that the function can be given.
Ask who decides the time, before and after the change.

acceptedIdeas: A seam where the test can supply any time, such as 08:59 or 17:00
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A seam where the test can supply any time, such as 08:59 or 17:00

questions.onCorrect: With the time as an argument, a test can pass 08:59 or 17:00 directly, and nothing has to wait for the right hour.

choices.label: A faster function, because the time is no longer looked up
A seam where the test can supply any time, such as 08:59 or 17:00
A record of how many times the clock was read
Nothing, because the function still depends on the time

misconceptions.feedback: The time is still looked up, but by whoever calls the function. What changes is who chooses it.
Nothing is recorded. The function is simply given the time, so the test chooses it.
It still needs a time, but the dependency now comes in from outside, and a test can choose it.

questions.prompt: A rule allows a discount when `10 <= quantity <= 99`. Which set of test cases pins down both ends of the range?
hints: Each end of the range is a boundary of its own.
Each boundary needs one value on each side of it.
questions.onCorrect: Each end of a range is a boundary of its own and needs one value just outside it and one just inside.

misconceptions.feedback: All four are inside the range, so a rule written with `<` in place of `<=` would pass every one of them.
0 and 200 are far outside the range, so a rule that let in 9 or 100 would still pass this set.
None of these is at an end of the range, so a limit set a little too high or too low would pass them.

questions.prompt: A project has these imports: the CLI adapter imports the use cases; the domain imports `requests`, an HTTP client library; the SMTP adapter imports the domain's `ReceiptSender` port; the domain imports `django`, a web framework; a test imports the domain. How many of these imports break the dependency rule?
hints: The rule is that dependencies point inward, toward the domain.
An import by the domain of something outside points outward.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The domain importing `requests` and the domain importing `django` point outward, so 2 break the rule.

questions.onCorrect: Two imports point outward, and both can be removed by giving the domain a port instead.

misconceptions.feedback: A test importing the domain points inward, which the rule allows.
Both `requests` and `django` are libraries outside the domain.

questions.prompt: A team adds a method to the domain's `Order` class that returns a web framework's `Response` object, so that the web layer can send it straight back. Which rule does this break?
hints: Source-code dependencies must point in a certain direction.
Ask whether the domain should need a web framework in order to run.
questions.onCorrect: The domain now cannot be built or tested without the web framework, though it should know nothing of it.

choices.label: The Liskov substitution principle
The rule of three
YAGNI
The dependency rule

misconceptions.feedback: That principle concerns a subtype standing in for its base type. This change makes the domain depend on a framework type.
The rule of three says when to remove repeated code. Nothing is repeated here, and the fault is the direction of a dependency.
YAGNI warns against building for needs that do not exist yet. This is a real dependency, and it points outward from the domain.

questions.prompt: An orders service and a stock service are deployed separately, but both read and write the same `stock` table. A developer wants to rename a column in that table. What has to happen?
hints: Ask which services have the column name written into their code.
Services get their independence only if each owns its own data.

acceptedIdeas: Both teams have to agree, because both services depend on the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both teams have to agree, because both services depend on the table

questions.onCorrect: Two services that share a table are not independent, because its layout can change only with the agreement of both.

choices.label: Both teams have to agree, because both services depend on the table
Only the stock team has to act, because the table is named after stock
Nothing beyond the edit, because separate deployment keeps the services independent
Only the team that runs the database server has to act

misconceptions.feedback: Table names do not decide who depends on a table. The orders service reads and writes it too, so a change to it reaches that service.
Deploying separately does not make the services independent while they share a table. Each is tied to the other's use of it.
The people who run the server do not know how each service uses the columns. The two services depend on the table, so the teams that own them have to agree.

questions.prompt: Which of these messages is an event?
hints: Names in the imperative ask for something.
An event reports something that has already happened.
questions.onCorrect: PaymentTaken is in the past tense because it reports a fact, and a fact cannot be refused.

choices.label: ReserveStock
PlaceOrder
CancelShipment
PaymentTaken

misconceptions.feedback: ReserveStock is in the imperative because it asks the stock service to do something, and the service may refuse. That makes it a command.
PlaceOrder asks for an order to be placed and can be refused, for example when the basket is empty. That makes it a command.
CancelShipment asks for something to be undone and can be refused once the shipment has left. That makes it a command.

questions.prompt: A new order has to reach billing, shipping and analytics today, and other teams add more listeners every few months. Which style suits it, and what does that style cost?
hints: Ask which style is easy to extend with a new listener.
The price of having no coordinator is that nobody holds the whole flow.

acceptedIdeas: Choreography, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Choreography, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place

questions.onCorrect: Each new listener only subscribes to the event, but nobody holds the whole flow, so it is harder to follow and to debug.

choices.label: Orchestration, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place
Orchestration, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on
Choreography, at the price of a flow that is hard to follow in one place
Choreography, at the price of a central service that every flow depends on

misconceptions.feedback: Orchestration keeps the flow in one place, so it is the easy one to follow. Its price is the central service that every flow depends on.
Orchestration is built for a few steps that rarely change. Here other teams keep adding listeners, and a coordinator would have to be edited for each.
Choreography has no central service. Its price is that nobody holds the whole flow, so the flow is harder to follow and to debug.

questions.prompt: An account's events are deposit 200, withdraw 75, deposit 25 and withdraw 60, in that order, from 0. What was the balance after the third event?
hints: Replay the events in order from 0, and stop after the third.
Deposits add and withdrawals subtract.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Replaying only the first three events gives 200 − 75 + 25 = 150. The fourth event had not yet happened.

questions.onCorrect: Replaying the log up to a point gives the state at that point, which is how a past state can be read.

misconceptions.feedback: That replays all four events. The question asks for the balance after the third.
That stops after the second event. The third, a deposit of 25, comes before the point asked about.
That adds every amount. Withdrawals subtract.

questions.prompt: Which change is backwards compatible for existing clients?
hints: Which change leaves everything the clients already use in place?
Clients that send nothing new must still be accepted.

acceptedIdeas: Accepting a new optional parameter in requests
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Accepting a new optional parameter in requests

questions.onCorrect: A request without the new parameter is accepted as before, so existing clients carry on.

choices.label: Accepting a new optional parameter in requests
Changing the unit of the `price` field from pence to pounds
Lowering the maximum request size from 1 MB to 100 KB
Making an existing optional field required

misconceptions.feedback: The field keeps its name and type, but its meaning has changed, so every client that reads it now gets a wrong value.
Requests that used to be accepted are now rejected, so this tightens validation, which breaks clients.
Clients that omitted the field are now rejected.

questions.prompt: A provider is renaming `qty` to `quantity` with expand and contract, and sends both names. Four of its five clients now read `quantity`. The fifth, from another company, has not replied. What should the provider do?
hints: The old name can go only when no client reads it.
Four clients have moved and one has not.

acceptedIdeas: Keep sending both names until the fifth client has moved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep sending both names until the fifth client has moved

questions.onCorrect: Until the last client moves, both names stay, and the provider carries the cost of sending both.

choices.label: Stop sending `qty` now, since most clients have moved
Keep sending both names until the fifth client has moved
Stop sending `qty` after a month, whether or not the fifth client has moved
Stop sending `quantity` and go back to `qty`

misconceptions.feedback: The fifth client still reads `qty`, so it breaks the day the name goes.
A deadline does not change what the fifth client reads. The old name can go only when no client reads it.
That undoes the migration the four clients have made, and the fifth will still not have moved.

questions.prompt: A provider adds a new allowed value, `refunded`, to a `status` field that used to be either `paid` or `pending`. Which description of this change is right?
hints: Ask what a client does when it meets a value it was never written for.
The safety of an addition depends on how the consumers read.

acceptedIdeas: It can break a client that assumed the old two values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It can break a client that assumed the old two values

questions.onCorrect: Adding a value is safe for a tolerant reader and breaking for a client that assumed the old set, so the provider has to know how its clients read.

choices.label: It breaks no client, because adding a value removes nothing
It breaks every client, because every client reads `status`
It can break a client that assumed the old two values

misconceptions.feedback: A client written for two values may stop on a third, so an addition can still break it.
A client that handles values it does not recognise carries on. Only clients that assumed the old set of values fail.

questions.prompt: Six changes are proposed: remove an endpoint, add an optional request parameter, rename a response field, change the error code for a missing item from 404 to 410, add a response field, and make a required request field optional. How many of them are breaking?
hints: Which of the six make a correct existing client fail?
The contract includes the errors a client may receive, as well as the fields.
Additions and relaxations leave existing clients working.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing an endpoint, renaming a response field and changing an error code that clients check are breaking, which makes 3. Adding an optional request parameter, adding a response field and making a required field optional only add or relax something.

questions.onCorrect: Additions and relaxations are usually safe, while removing, renaming or changing what a client relies on is not.

misconceptions.feedback: That misses one. A client that checks for a particular error code breaks when the code changes.
One of those four only relaxes a rule, so it accepts everything it accepted before.
Adding an optional parameter, adding a response field and making a required field optional leave existing clients working.

questions.prompt: In a container diagram, an arrow joins the booking API to its database. Which label for the arrow follows the diagram hygiene rules?
hints: Every arrow should say what it carries.
Look for the label that names the data and the way it travels.
questions.onCorrect: Naming the data and the protocol tells the reader what crosses the arrow without anyone having to explain.

choices.label: Uses the booking database
Reads and writes bookings (SQL)
Connects to the database
Database access layer

misconceptions.feedback: This says the boxes are related but not what the arrow carries, so the reader still has to guess whether it is a request, an event or a copy.
This only says that the boxes are joined, which the arrow already shows.
This names a kind of box and not what travels along the arrow.

questions.prompt: An engineer is about to change how the booking API validates tickets and wants to see the API's inner parts. Which C4 level fits best?
hints: The engineer wants the parts inside one container.
Pick the level that opens a single container.
questions.onCorrect: Components is the level for someone about to change one container, and code can be added for the one component they will edit.

choices.label: Components
Containers
System context
Code

misconceptions.feedback: A container diagram shows the API as one box among the other runnable parts, so its inner parts do not appear.
Context treats the whole system as one box, so the API does not appear at all.
Code shows the classes inside a component, which is more detail than the engineer needs before knowing which parts of the API to open.

questions.prompt: Which list gives the four C4 levels from the widest view to the narrowest?
hints: Each level opens up one part of the level before it.
questions.onCorrect: The fourth level, code, is rarely drawn by hand because it can be generated from the source.

choices.label: Containers, system context, components, code
System context, components, containers, code
System context, containers, components, code
System context, containers, code, components

misconceptions.feedback: System context is the widest view, with the whole system as one box, so it comes before containers.
Containers open the system once, and components open one container, so containers come before components.
Code is the narrowest level, the classes inside a component, so it comes last.

questions.prompt: Option A scores 8, 5 and 6 on performance, cost and simplicity, and option B scores 6, 9 and 9. The weights are now performance 0.6, cost 0.2 and simplicity 0.2. Which option has the higher weighted total?
hints: Work out each option's total with the new weights.
Multiply each score by its own weight and add the three products.
questions.onCorrect: B totals 7.2 and A totals 7.0, so the ranking holds with these weights, although A is much closer than it was.

choices.label: Option A
Option B
They tie

misconceptions.feedback: A's total rises to 7.0 as performance counts for more, but B's total is 7.2, so B is still ahead.
The totals are 7.0 and 7.2, so they do not tie.

flashcards.front: What is the shortest description of software architecture used in this course?
flashcards.back: Architecture is the set of decisions about structure that are costly to change later.

flashcards.front: A quality attribute scenario has how many parts?
flashcards.back: Six: source, stimulus, artefact, environment, response and response measure.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six parts.

flashcards.front: Which part of a scenario holds the number a test compares against?
flashcards.back: The response measure, which is why it turns a wish into a requirement.

flashcards.front: How many links join n modules when every module depends on every other?
flashcards.back: n × (n − 1) ÷ 2, so 6 modules have 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 × 5 ÷ 2 = 15, for 6 modules.

flashcards.front: What is feature envy?
flashcards.back: A method that uses another class's data more than its own, which suggests it belongs on that class.

flashcards.front: Why does a class that formats invoices and also sends email have low cohesion?
flashcards.back: It has two unrelated reasons to change, so a change to one risks the other.

flashcards.front: What is a leaky abstraction?
flashcards.back: An interface that exposes an implementation detail, so that callers come to depend on it.

flashcards.front: What did Parnas say a module should hide?
flashcards.back: A design decision that is difficult or likely to change, so that a change to it stays inside one module.

flashcards.front: What does a leading underscore on a Python name mean?
flashcards.back: It is a convention marking the name as internal, and the language does not enforce it.

flashcards.front: Which principle says code written for a base type must keep working when given a subtype?
flashcards.back: Liskov substitution: code written for the base type keeps working when given the subtype, so the subtype must honour the base type's behaviour.

flashcards.front: Which four-letter acronym warns against building for needs you do not have yet?
flashcards.back: YAGNI, short for “you aren't gonna need it”, since the guessed need is often wrong and the code has to be kept anyway.

flashcards.front: Why are the SOLID principles heuristics rather than laws?
flashcards.back: Applying them mechanically adds abstraction that can cost more in complexity than it saves.

flashcards.front: What is composition?
flashcards.back: Building behaviour by holding other objects and delegating to them, instead of inheriting from them.

flashcards.front: Three transports and three formats: how many subclasses does inheritance need for every pair?
flashcards.back: 3 × 3 = 9, against 3 + 3 = 6 parts with composition.

flashcards.front: In one sentence, when should you inherit and when should you compose?
flashcards.back: Inherit for a substitutable specialisation, and compose to reuse behaviour.

flashcards.front: Which pattern lets a subject notify subscribers of a change without knowing what they do?
flashcards.back: Observer: the subject holds a list and calls each subscriber in turn.

flashcards.front: How many patterns did the 1994 book Design Patterns describe?
flashcards.back: 23 patterns, by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The book describes 23 patterns.

flashcards.front: When is applying a pattern a mistake?
flashcards.back: When no problem exists yet, because the pattern then adds indirection without any benefit.

flashcards.front: What is ubiquitous language?
flashcards.back: One vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts, used in the conversation and in the code.

flashcards.front: What separates an entity from a value object?
flashcards.back: An entity is identified by an identity that persists as its data changes, while a value object is defined entirely by its data.

flashcards.front: What is the boundary called inside which a term has one meaning?
flashcards.back: A bounded context.

flashcards.front: What is a seam?
flashcards.back: A place where behaviour can be replaced without editing the code, such as an argument that supplies a dependency.

flashcards.front: Which kind of test double returns canned answers?
flashcards.back: A stub returns canned answers, while a fake works in a small way and a mock records calls.

flashcards.front: A rule allows entry when `age >= 18`. How many boundary cases does it need?
flashcards.back: Two: 17, which is refused, and 18, which is accepted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cases are 17 and 18.

flashcards.front: Which word names the interface the domain defines for something it needs?
flashcards.back: A port is the interface that the domain defines for something it needs or offers, which adapters implement or call.

flashcards.front: Which rule says that source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain?
flashcards.back: The dependency rule says that source-code dependencies point inward, toward the domain, and never outward to frameworks.

flashcards.front: Why can a layered design still be tightly coupled?
flashcards.back: If everything depends on the data layer's shapes, a change to the database reaches every layer above it.

flashcards.front: Which style is one deployable unit with enforced module boundaries?
flashcards.back: A modular monolith.

flashcards.front: Five services in a chain are each 99.9% available. What is the chain's availability, in percent, to one decimal place?
flashcards.back: 0.999 to the power 5 is 0.995, so 99.5%.

flashcards.front: Why do services that share one database table fail to be independent?
flashcards.back: A change to the table's schema must be agreed by every service that reads it, so they are coupled through the table.

flashcards.front: How does an event's name differ from a command's?
flashcards.back: An event is named in the past tense, such as OrderPlaced, and a command in the imperative, such as PlaceOrder.

flashcards.front: Event sourcing keeps a log of what, instead of storing the current state?
flashcards.back: The sequence of events, with the state rebuilt by replaying them.

flashcards.front: Events: deposit 50, withdraw 20, deposit 5. What is the balance after replay?
What is a breaking change?
flashcards.back: A change that makes a correct existing client fail, such as removing or renaming a field, changing a type, or tightening validation.

flashcards.front: Which technique adds the new form beside the old, moves clients across, and only then removes the old form?
flashcards.back: Expand and contract, done over three releases.

flashcards.front: Why is adding a field not always safe?
flashcards.back: A strict consumer that rejects fields it does not know will fail when a new one appears.

flashcards.front: Name the four C4 levels from widest to narrowest.
flashcards.back: Context, containers, components, code.

flashcards.front: Is a C4 container the same as a Docker container?
flashcards.back: No. A C4 container is any separately runnable unit, such as a web app, a mobile app or a database.

flashcards.front: How many C4 levels are there?
flashcards.back: Four, and each answers a different question for a different audience.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are four levels.

flashcards.front: What five fields does an architecture decision record have?
flashcards.back: Title, status, context, decision, consequences.

flashcards.front: What is a fitness function?
flashcards.back: An automated check that a chosen architectural property still holds, such as no domain module importing the web framework.

flashcards.front: A scores 8, 5, 6 with weights 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. What is the weighted total?
Which expression of Ca and Ce gives a module's instability?
flashcards.back: I = Ce / (Ca + Ce), where Ce counts outgoing dependencies and Ca counts incoming ones.

flashcards.front: What is the strangler pattern?
flashcards.back: A facade routes requests to new code one slice at a time, until the old system has no work left and can be removed.

flashcards.front: Why write a characterisation test before refactoring untested code?
flashcards.back: It records what the code does today, so that an unintended change can be detected.
